clinicalPearls: Often discovered incidentally as a persistently low serum urate in an otherwise well person.
A high fractional excretion of urate is the diagnostic hallmark and separates renal wasting from urate underproduction.
Two principal forms exist: type 1 from SLC22A12 (URAT1) and type 2 from SLC2A9 (GLUT9), the latter tending to cause more profound hypouricaemia.
Exercise-induced acute kidney injury, characteristically after short bursts of anaerobic exertion, is the most important complication.
Uric acid urolithiasis is more frequent, and good hydration is protective.
URAT1 founder variants are common in East Asian, notably Japanese and Korean, populations.
Distinguish from hereditary xanthinuria, in which serum urate is low but urinary urate is also low and xanthine accumulates.
Avoiding strenuous anaerobic exercise and dehydration reduces the risk of acute kidney injury.
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary renal hypouricaemia results from loss-of-function mutations in the tubular transporters that normally reclaim filtered urate. Type 1 disease is caused by mutations in SLC22A12, which encodes URAT1, the apical urate-anion exchanger of the proximal tubule responsible for the bulk of urate reabsorption; type 2 disease is caused by mutations in SLC2A9, which encodes GLUT9, the high-capacity voltage-driven transporter that moves urate across the basolateral membrane. Impaired reabsorption markedly increases the fractional excretion of urate and lowers the serum concentration, with GLUT9 defects producing the more severe hypouricaemia. The loss of urate, a major circulating antioxidant, together with a high urinary urate load, is thought to predispose affected individuals to exercise-induced acute kidney injury — postulated to involve oxidative stress and renal vasoconstriction after anaerobic exercise — and to uric acid stone formation. Renal function is otherwise typically well preserved between episodes.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi syndrome, in which hypouricaemia accompanies glycosuria, aminoaciduria and phosphaturia.
Hereditary xanthinuria (xanthine dehydrogenase deficiency) with low urinary urate and xanthine stones.
Molybdenum cofactor deficiency and other purine-metabolism disorders.
Drug-induced hypouricaemia from uricosurics such as benzbromarone, from losartan, high-dose salicylates or SGLT2 inhibitors.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis and other acquired causes of a low serum urate.
Severe liver disease or malignancy lowering the serum urate.
additionalInvestigations: Serum urate, confirmed on repeat testing.
Urinary urate with calculation of the fractional excretion of urate.
Renal tract imaging for stones and nephrocalcinosis.
Urinary xanthine and hypoxanthine to exclude xanthinuria.
Screen of proximal tubular function to exclude a generalised Fanconi syndrome.
Genetic testing of SLC22A12 and SLC2A9.
redFlags: Acute kidney injury or severe loin pain developing after exercise.
Features of a generalised proximal tubulopathy, pointing away from isolated renal hypouricaemia.
Oliguria or a rapid decline in renal function following anaerobic exertion.
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally benign with well-preserved long-term renal function. The main threats are recurrent uric acid stones and repeated episodes of exercise-induced acute kidney injury, both of which are largely preventable.
pitfalls: Dismissing a low serum urate as a laboratory artefact rather than investigating it.
Failing to link post-exercise acute kidney injury to the underlying urate-handling defect.
Confusing renal hypouricaemia with xanthinuria or with a generalised Fanconi syndrome.
Using nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs during an episode of exercise-induced acute kidney injury.
Assuming an asymptomatic patient carries no risk and omitting advice on hydration and exercise.
references: Reviews of renal urate transport and inherited hypouricaemia
